quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: When a patient moves between hospital shifts, vital details can be lost in a rushed conversation. One hospital introduced a short checklist covering medication, allergies and pending tests. Nurses were sceptical because it added a minute to every handover. After six months, however, incident reports about missed information had fallen by almost half. The hospital now trains new staff to use the checklist before they treat a single patient.
options: Nurses backed the checklist from the start because it saved time at handovers.
A checklist covering allergies and tests was introduced for newly trained nursing staff.
The hospital dropped the checklist after incident reports failed to improve within six months.
A simple handover checklist reduced errors, despite nurses' first doubts about the extra time.
quests.correctAnswer: A simple handover checklist reduced errors, despite nurses' first doubts about the extra time.
quests.hint: Notice how the nurses' first reaction differs from the later evidence.
quests.explanation: Doubt about the added minute was answered by a large fall in incidents. The wrong options reverse the nurses' attitude, the results or the scope of the checklist.
keyPoints: Vital details were being lost when patients changed shifts.
A checklist covering medication, allergies and tests was introduced.
Incident reports fell by almost half, and training now includes it.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Many graduates leave university with large loans, and repayment plans are complicated. Some economists argue that debt discourages young people from choosing lower-paid but socially valuable careers. Others reply that graduates still earn more on average and that repayments depend on income, so they are not like ordinary debts. Surveys suggest that students' worry is greater than the actual monthly burden. Nevertheless, confusion about the terms may itself affect their choices.
options: Surveys show that students' anxiety is lower than the monthly burden that they really face.
Repayments are fixed amounts, so graduates on low salaries pay the same as high earners.
Student debt worries may exceed the actual burden and still shape career decisions.
Economists agree that student loans make graduates poorer than people who did not attend university.
quests.correctAnswer: Student debt worries may exceed the actual burden and still shape career decisions.
quests.hint: Compare what the economists say with what the surveys and the final sentence add.
quests.explanation: The paragraph balances the claim that debt harms career choice against evidence that the burden is manageable, then notes confusion may matter anyway. The wrong options overstate agreement, reverse how repayment works or reverse the survey.
keyPoints: Graduates carry large loans with complicated repayment terms.
Some see debt discouraging valuable careers, while others note income-based repayment.
Worry seems greater than the burden, but confusion may still influence choices.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Bicycle theft in the city has fallen by a third since the council installed locked cycle pods near the station. Users pay a small monthly fee and open the pod with a card. Critics say the pods take up pavement space that pedestrians need. Planners reply that each pod holds six bicycles in the space of one parked car. Commuters, meanwhile, report that they now cycle to the station more often because they feel their bikes are safe.
options: Locked cycle pods have cut theft and encouraged cycling, though space use is questioned.
Commuters now cycle less often because they fear that their bicycles will be stolen.
Each pod takes up the space of six parked cars, which pedestrians say is excessive.
Cycle pods are free for anyone who wants to store a bicycle near the station.
quests.correctAnswer: Locked cycle pods have cut theft and encouraged cycling, though space use is questioned.
quests.hint: Before choosing, check which figures are attached to which objects.
quests.explanation: The pods reduce theft and boost cycling, while the criticism about space is answered by the six-bikes-per-car comparison. The wrong options reverse the fee, the space ratio and commuters' behaviour.
keyPoints: Bicycle theft fell by a third after locked pods were installed.
Critics complain about pavement space, but each pod holds six bikes in one car's space.
Commuters cycle to the station more because they feel their bikes are safe.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Every autumn, fruit farms in the valley rely on seasonal workers from abroad. Many are housed in crowded caravans, and some pay high rents for basic beds. Inspectors have found unsafe wiring and blocked exits at several sites. The farm owners' association says it wants better housing but notes that supermarkets pay too little to cover the cost. Worker groups reply that supermarkets and farms share the responsibility and should agree on minimum standards together.
options: Inspectors found that farm housing in the valley meets basic safety standards.
Worker groups say supermarkets alone bear responsibility for improving worker housing.
Farm owners refuse to improve housing even if supermarkets paid more.
Poor seasonal-worker housing has become an argument about who should pay for improvements.
quests.correctAnswer: Poor seasonal-worker housing has become an argument about who should pay for improvements.
quests.hint: Distinguish the problem itself from the debate about responsibility for it.
quests.explanation: After describing unsafe conditions, the paragraph shows that owners, supermarkets and worker groups place the cost and blame differently. The wrong options deny the problems, exaggerate owners' refusal or narrow the blame.
keyPoints: Seasonal workers live in crowded, sometimes unsafe farm housing.
Owners want improvement but blame low supermarket payments.
Worker groups want farms and supermarkets to set minimum standards jointly.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A heritage railway in the hills survives on volunteers who drive the steam engines, repair the track and serve tea in the station café. Its income covers running costs but not major repairs. Last year, the boiler needed replacing, and the railway launched a crowd-funding campaign that raised the money in six weeks. Volunteers say such support shows people care about more than nostalgia. The railway now hopes to use the goodwill to fund a museum of railway history.
options: A volunteer-run railway used public goodwill to fund a costly repair and hopes to expand.
The railway earns enough from ticket sales to pay for major repairs itself.
Crowd-funding for the boiler took six months to reach its target, which discouraged volunteers.
Volunteers believe that visitors come out of nostalgia for steam, not community feeling.
quests.correctAnswer: A volunteer-run railway used public goodwill to fund a costly repair and hopes to expand.
quests.hint: Follow how the railway's limited income leads to a public appeal and a new ambition.
quests.explanation: Regular income cannot cover big repairs, so public donations paid for the boiler, and the railway wants to build on that support. The wrong options reverse the income, the speed of the campaign and the volunteers' comment.
keyPoints: Volunteers run and maintain a hillside steam railway.
Its income covers running costs but not a new boiler.
A six-week crowd-funding campaign succeeded, and a museum is now planned.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Scientific papers are usually reviewed by other experts before publication. Reviewers work unpaid, and delays can last months. Critics say the process is slow and sometimes fails to catch errors or fraud. Defenders argue that it still filters out most weak studies, and that no better system has been found. Some journals now publish reviewers' comments alongside articles, hoping that transparency will improve quality and encourage more careful reading.
options: Critics claim that peer review catches errors and fraud before publication occurs.
Journals have abandoned review and now publish new studies without expert checks.
Peer review is flawed and valuable and some journals are making it more transparent.
Reviewers are well paid for their work, which explains why reviews are usually so quick.
quests.correctAnswer: Peer review is flawed and valuable and some journals are making it more transparent.
quests.hint: Test each option against both the criticism and the defence.
quests.explanation: The paragraph presents peer review's shortcomings, a defence of its usefulness and a reform aimed at openness. The wrong options reverse payment, exaggerate the process's success or claim it has ended.
keyPoints: Experts review papers before publication, but unpaid work causes delays.
Critics point to missed errors, while defenders say it filters weak studies.
Some journals publish reviewers' comments to increase transparency.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: In a busy restaurant kitchen, each cook has a defined role: one prepares sauces, another grills and a third assembles desserts. The head chef calls out orders, and each cook repeats them to confirm. It sounds rigid, but it prevents mistakes when tickets are arriving every few seconds. Junior cooks rise through the roles over several years. Chefs say the system works because everyone knows exactly who is responsible for what.
options: Cooks in the kitchen choose their own tasks freely as each new order arrives.
A restaurant kitchen depends on defined roles and clear communication to work under pressure.
Junior cooks are moved between roles within minutes so that they learn faster.
The head chef prepares each dish personally to avoid mistakes on the busiest nights.
quests.correctAnswer: A restaurant kitchen depends on defined roles and clear communication to work under pressure.
quests.hint: Imagine removing the roles: which idea would the paragraph lose?
quests.explanation: Fixed roles and spoken confirmation keep service accurate when it is fast. The wrong options describe free choice, a single cook or role changes within seconds.
keyPoints: Cooks in a busy kitchen have fixed roles.
The head chef calls orders, and cooks repeat them back.
The structure prevents mistakes because responsibility is clear.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Much of the internet's software is built by volunteers who maintain open-source projects in their free time. Companies use the tools in their products, but few contribute money. When a serious flaw appeared in one widely used library, it turned out that a single unpaid developer was responsible for fixing it. Some firms have since started funding maintainers directly. Others argue that public money should support software that so many services depend on.
options: Companies pay volunteers well for most of the open-source tools that they use daily.
A team of paid engineers repaired the widely used library's serious flaw within days.
Critical open-source software relies on unpaid maintainers, prompting calls for funding.
Firms have agreed that public money is unnecessary for maintaining shared software.
quests.correctAnswer: Critical open-source software relies on unpaid maintainers, prompting calls for funding.
quests.hint: Trace the problem, the incident that exposed it and the proposed remedies.
quests.explanation: The incident showed how much depends on unpaid work, so some firms and advocates are pushing for funding. The wrong options reverse who pays, who fixed the flaw and what firms think.
keyPoints: Volunteers maintain open-source projects that companies widely use.
One library flaw revealed dependence on a single unpaid developer.
Some firms fund maintainers, and others want public money.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Remote villages struggle to attract doctors, who prefer the higher pay and social life of cities. A regional scheme now offers medical students free tuition if they agree to practise in a rural area for five years. Similar schemes abroad have kept many graduates in villages beyond their contracts. Early participants say they were surprised by how varied the work is and how quickly they became trusted. However, several worry about feeling professionally isolated, so the scheme is adding video links to city specialists.
options: A rural doctor scheme is drawing graduates to villages, with support added against isolation.
Participants found village work dull and impersonal, so many plan to leave early.
Rural doctors receive the highest salaries in the region, which explains the scheme's success.
Video links were introduced to replace the five-year commitment that graduates dislike.
quests.correctAnswer: A rural doctor scheme is drawing graduates to villages, with support added against isolation.
quests.hint: Identify the incentive, the participants' experience and the remaining worry.
quests.explanation: Free tuition brings doctors to the villages, the work turns out to be rewarding, and isolation is being tackled with technology. The wrong options reverse pay, experience and the purpose of the video links.
keyPoints: Villages find it hard to attract doctors away from cities.
A scheme trades free tuition for five years of rural practice.
Participants enjoy the work but fear isolation, so video links are added.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A secondary school trialled sound-absorbing ceiling panels in its noisiest classrooms. Teachers reported that they no longer had to raise their voices, and pupils could hear instructions without asking for repeats. Pupils in the trial rooms also said they felt less tired by the end of the day. Test scores in the trial rooms rose slightly, though the improvement was too small to prove the panels were the cause. The school has decided to fit more rooms anyway, arguing that quieter lessons are worth having regardless of the marks.
options: Quieter classrooms won the school's support even without proof of higher scores.
The school abandoned the trial when test scores failed to improve.
The panels proved that quieter rooms raise pupils' test scores.
Teachers had to raise their voices even more after the panels were fitted.
quests.correctAnswer: Quieter classrooms won the school's support even without proof of higher scores.
quests.hint: Give attention to what the evidence proves and what it does not.
quests.explanation: The benefits for teaching are clear, the effect on scores is uncertain, and the school proceeds for the first reason. The wrong options claim proof, reverse the effect on voices or reverse the decision.
keyPoints: Sound-absorbing panels were tested in noisy classrooms.
Teachers spoke more easily and pupils heard instructions better.
Score gains were too small to prove causation, but more rooms will be fitted.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Coffee plants traditionally grow beneath taller trees, which shade the crop and provide habitat for birds. Many farmers have removed the shade to plant more bushes and boost short-term yields. The change makes the plants more exposed to heat and disease, so farmers often use more chemicals. Some cooperatives now pay a premium for shade-grown coffee, and buyers advertise it as bird-friendly. Whether the premium is large enough to change farmers' habits remains uncertain.
options: The premium has already persuaded most farmers to replant shade trees across the valley.
Cooperatives pay less for shade-grown coffee than for sun-grown coffee, discouraging shade.
Farmers who remove shade trees use fewer chemicals because the plants grow more strongly.
Shade-grown coffee helps wildlife, and a price premium may not change farmers' habits.
quests.correctAnswer: Shade-grown coffee helps wildlife, and a price premium may not change farmers' habits.
quests.hint: Contrast the short-term motive with the long-term cost and the incentive offered.
quests.explanation: Removing shade brings quick gains but greater risks, and the premium is an attempt to reverse this trend whose success is unclear. The wrong options reverse chemical use, the premium and the outcome.
keyPoints: Coffee traditionally grows under shade trees that help birds.
Removing shade raises yields but increases heat stress and chemical use.
A premium for shade-grown coffee may or may not change farmers' habits.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Architects are designing office towers made largely from engineered timber. Wood stores carbon rather than releasing it, and prefabricated panels can be assembled faster than concrete. Fire safety is a common worry, but thick timber chars on the outside and protects the core for a long time. Insurers remain cautious, and building codes in many countries still limit the height of wooden structures. Advocates say that regulations will change as evidence accumulates.
options: Timber towers release more carbon than comparable concrete buildings do over their lifetime.
Timber towers store carbon and build quickly, but rules and insurers lag behind.
Thick timber burns through quickly and offers little protection for the building's core.
Insurers and building codes have already welcomed wooden skyscrapers in most countries.
quests.correctAnswer: Timber towers store carbon and build quickly, but rules and insurers lag behind.
quests.hint: Pick the option that handles both the promise and the obstacles.
quests.explanation: The paragraph lists benefits, answers a safety concern and admits that rules and insurers lag behind. The wrong options reverse carbon, fire and regulation statements.
keyPoints: Engineered-timber towers store carbon and go up quickly.
Thick timber chars and protects the core in a fire.
Insurers and codes remain cautious, but advocates expect change.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Several museums now open late on Friday nights with music, bars and short talks. The events draw younger visitors who rarely attend in the daytime. Curators enjoy the energy but worry that crowds and drinks pose risks for delicate objects. Some galleries are therefore closed to the night audience or fitted with barriers. Revenue from tickets and bars has helped fund an education programme for schools, which the museum says would otherwise have been cut.
options: Late openings bring young visitors and income, if fragile objects are protected.
Income from the bars is spent on building barriers around the galleries.
Night events have replaced the museum's daytime visitors, who now stay away.
Curators fear that nobody will attend late-night events, so they limit the programme.
quests.correctAnswer: Late openings bring young visitors and income, if fragile objects are protected.
quests.hint: Notice the benefit, the worry and the way the museum responds to it.
quests.explanation: The events bring new visitors and money, with adjustments made for safety. The wrong options replace the daytime audience, reverse the curators' concern or misdirect the income.
keyPoints: Museums hold late Friday events with music and talks.
They attract younger visitors, but crowds threaten fragile objects.
Income funds a schools programme that would otherwise be cut.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Teenagers' body clocks shift later during puberty, so many struggle to fall asleep before eleven and to wake before eight. Yet most schools start at half past eight or earlier. Several districts that moved start times later reported improved attendance, fewer accidents among young drivers and higher marks. Transport costs and after-school activities complicated the change. Even so, doctors continue to recommend later starts for secondary schools, since sleep affects health as well as learning.
options: Doctors recommend later starts mainly because they would reduce school transport costs.
Later starts suit teenagers' sleep and bring benefits, with practical difficulties.
Teenagers naturally fall asleep earlier than younger children, so early starts suit them.
Districts that started school later saw poorer attendance and lower marks than before.
quests.correctAnswer: Later starts suit teenagers' sleep and bring benefits, with practical difficulties.
quests.hint: Separate the biological reason from the evidence and the obstacles.
quests.explanation: Puberty shifts sleep, later starts help several outcomes, and cost and logistics are challenges. The wrong options reverse the body-clock shift, the outcomes and the doctors' reason.
keyPoints: Teenagers' body clocks shift later, but schools start early.
Districts with later starts saw better attendance, safety and marks.
Transport and activities complicate the change, but doctors still advise it.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Warehouses are adding robots that carry shelves to workers instead of workers walking to shelves. The change cuts walking time and increases the number of orders a person can pack. Some staff say the work has become faster and more repetitive, leaving little chance to talk. Managers respond that the robots take on the heaviest lifting, which reduces back injuries. Unions ask that productivity gains be shared through shorter shifts or higher pay.
options: Staff enjoy the work more now that it is slower and more varied.
Robots have replaced warehouse workers on the packing floor, according to managers.
Unions want the productivity gains to go to managers and shareholders.
Robots raise warehouse productivity and workers want a fair share of the gains.
quests.correctAnswer: Robots raise warehouse productivity and workers want a fair share of the gains.
quests.hint: Give the managers' benefits, the workers' complaint and the union's request in one idea.
quests.explanation: Automation improves efficiency and safety but changes the character of work, so unions seek a fair share. The wrong options claim total replacement, reverse worker reactions or reverse the union's demand.
keyPoints: Robots bring shelves to workers, cutting walking time.
Work is faster but more repetitive, though lifting injuries decline.
Unions want the gains shared through shorter shifts or higher pay.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Welsh was spoken by fewer and fewer children until the 1980s, when schools began teaching in the language. Today, about a quarter of pupils are educated mainly in Welsh, and many come from homes where it is not spoken. Television and music have also helped to make it fashionable. Bilingual road signs and public services have reinforced its everyday use. However, in some rural communities, where Welsh is traditionally strongest, young people leave for jobs elsewhere, so the language's future depends on more than schools.
options: Welsh has recovered through schools and media, and rural decline threatens it.
Welsh has been taught in schools throughout, so its numbers have not declined.
Most pupils who learn Welsh come from homes where it is spoken daily.
Rural communities now have more young Welsh speakers than they have ever had.
quests.correctAnswer: Welsh has recovered through schools and media, and rural decline threatens it.
quests.hint: Recognise a success story with a warning at the end.
quests.explanation: Education and culture revived the language, but the loss of young people from strongholds is a threat. The wrong options ignore the earlier decline, reverse the pupils' backgrounds or deny the rural problem.
keyPoints: Welsh declined among children until schools began teaching in it.
About a quarter of pupils now learn mainly in Welsh, and media help.
Young people leaving rural areas threatens the language's future.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Owners of flat roofs in the city can now lease them to a solar company at no upfront cost. The company installs the panels and sells the electricity to the grid, paying the owner a small rent. Building owners like the extra income, and residents in the same block are offered cheaper power. Yet some older buildings cannot carry the weight without expensive reinforcement, which limits how many roofs qualify. The city hopes that simpler regulations will encourage more roofs to join.
options: Flat roofs in the city are strong enough to carry solar panels safely.
Owners must pay the solar company to install panels on their roofs before renting.
Solar roof leasing benefits owners and residents, and structural limits restrict the scheme.
Residents are charged more for electricity than other households in the same block.
quests.correctAnswer: Solar roof leasing benefits owners and residents, and structural limits restrict the scheme.
quests.hint: Check who pays, who earns and what restricts participation.
quests.explanation: The company funds the installation, owners and residents benefit, and roof strength restricts the number of sites. The wrong options reverse the payment, the suitability of roofs and the price for residents.
keyPoints: Owners can lease flat roofs to a solar company at no upfront cost.
The company sells electricity, pays rent and offers residents cheaper power.
Weak older roofs limit participation, so the city hopes to ease regulations.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: When one Scandinavian country required companies to publish salary ranges in job advertisements, the gap between men's and women's pay narrowed slightly. Job seekers could compare offers and negotiate more confidently. Employers complained that the rule was time-consuming and that it might discourage them from rewarding exceptional employees. Researchers say early results are promising but that other factors, such as childcare costs, also affect the pay gap. They therefore advise caution in claiming that transparency alone is the solution.
options: Employers welcomed the rule because it was quick and easy for them to follow.
Salary transparency narrows the pay gap somewhat and is not a full solution.
Pay transparency closed the gap between men's and women's pay within a year.
Researchers say childcare costs have little effect on the pay gap.
quests.correctAnswer: Salary transparency narrows the pay gap somewhat and is not a full solution.
quests.hint: Watch for a conclusion that claims more than researchers do.
quests.explanation: Evidence suggests transparency helps, yet the researchers stress that other causes also matter. The wrong options claim a full solution, reverse employers' reaction or deny other factors.
keyPoints: Publishing salary ranges slightly narrowed the pay gap.
Job seekers negotiated more confidently, though employers complained.
Researchers warn that transparency alone cannot solve the whole problem.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Since AI writing tools became widely available, universities worry about students submitting work that is not their own. Software that detects machine-written text is unreliable and sometimes accuses honest students. Some lecturers have therefore returned to oral exams and in-class writing. Others encourage students to use the tools openly and then reflect on what they learned. Everyone agrees that assessment must measure understanding, but they disagree about how to do it without penalising the innocent.
options: Detection software reliably identifies machine-written work, so problems are solved.
AI writing tools force universities to rethink assessment, with no agreed solution yet.
Oral exams have been abandoned in favour of take-home essays across most universities.
Lecturers have agreed to ban writing tools from assessments.
quests.correctAnswer: AI writing tools force universities to rethink assessment, with no agreed solution yet.
quests.hint: Compare the different responses and what they have in common.
quests.explanation: The paragraph lists responses to a shared problem and ends with a disagreement about method. The wrong options claim perfect detection, universal bans or the abandonment of oral exams.
keyPoints: AI tools worry universities about work that is not the students' own.
Detection software is unreliable, so some lecturers use oral exams while others allow open use.
All want assessments to measure understanding fairly, but they differ on how.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Volunteers keep many community organisations running, yet organisers report that burnout is common. Enthusiastic people take on too many tasks, and few are ready to share them. Some groups now set a maximum number of hours per volunteer and rotate leadership roles each year. Newcomers are given small, clear tasks instead of open-ended requests. One organiser says the aim is to make helping sustainable, so people still want to return after the first months.
options: Volunteer groups are limiting workloads and sharing roles to prevent burnout and keep helpers.
Leadership roles stay with one experienced volunteer for many years to keep continuity.
Groups give newcomers large open-ended tasks to keep them engaged for longer.
Volunteers rarely experience burnout because community organisations already share tasks evenly.
quests.correctAnswer: Volunteer groups are limiting workloads and sharing roles to prevent burnout and keep helpers.
quests.hint: Find the problem and the group of remedies together.
quests.explanation: Overload leads to burnout, and the remedies are limits, rotation and clearer tasks. The wrong options deny burnout, reverse the tasks given to newcomers or the leadership practice.
keyPoints: Volunteers often take on too much and burn out.
Some groups cap hours and rotate leadership yearly.
Newcomers receive small, clear tasks to encourage them to return.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Local newspapers have closed in hundreds of towns as advertising moved online. Without reporters at council meetings, residents find it harder to learn how public money is spent. Research in several countries has linked newspaper closures to lower voter turnout and less scrutiny of local officials. A few communities have responded by launching non-profit news sites funded by donations. Their reach is smaller, but editors say that even modest coverage keeps local decisions in view.
options: Non-profit news sites now reach larger audiences than the newspapers they have replaced.
Newspapers have closed because reporters attend too many council meetings and cost too much.
Newspaper closures weaken scrutiny of officials, and non-profit sites try to fill the gap.
Research links newspaper closures to higher voter turnout and closer scrutiny of officials.
quests.correctAnswer: Newspaper closures weaken scrutiny of officials, and non-profit sites try to fill the gap.
quests.hint: Trace how one change leads to another, then to a response.
quests.explanation: Lost advertising closed papers, and the loss reduced scrutiny and participation, prompting small non-profit replacements. The wrong options reverse the cause, the turnout finding and the comparison of reach.
keyPoints: Advertising moved online, and many local papers closed.
Studies link closures to lower turnout and less scrutiny.
Non-profit news sites offer modest but useful coverage.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A school introduced a free lunch for every pupil rather than only for children from poorer families. Previously, some eligible children avoided the meal because they felt embarrassed. Take-up rose sharply, and teachers noticed better concentration in the afternoons. The scheme costs more, and critics ask why wealthy families should benefit. Supporters answer that a single scheme removes stigma and is cheaper to administer than checking eligibility.
options: Supporters argue that checking eligibility is cheaper than running a single universal scheme.
Free lunches are still offered to children from poorer families in the school.
Universal free lunches raised take-up and removed stigma and critics question the extra cost.
Take-up fell because wealthy families avoided the school meal once it became free.
quests.correctAnswer: Universal free lunches raised take-up and removed stigma and critics question the extra cost.
quests.hint: Give both what the change achieved and the argument about it.
quests.explanation: Making lunch universal ended embarrassment and improved concentration, and the debate is about fairness of cost. The wrong options reverse eligibility, take-up and supporters' argument.
keyPoints: The school offers a free lunch to every pupil.
Embarrassment kept some eligible children away before, but take-up rose.
Critics question the cost, and supporters cite reduced stigma and simpler administration.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Food banks began as emergency stopgaps but have become permanent fixtures in many towns. Volunteers say that more working families now rely on them, especially when rent or heating costs increase. Some banks have added advice services to help people claim benefits or manage debts. Organisers appreciate the public generosity but say that donated tins cannot solve underlying poverty. They want national policy to address the reasons why so many people need help.
options: Advice services were closed because donations from the public are now sufficient.
Food banks are now permanent, and organisers want policy to tackle the causes.
Organisers believe donated food can solve poverty if enough is collected.
Food banks are used by people without jobs who rely on donations.
quests.correctAnswer: Food banks are now permanent, and organisers want policy to tackle the causes.
quests.hint: Move from what food banks do to what organisers believe is needed.
quests.explanation: Food banks are no longer temporary, and their organisers argue that policy must deal with the root problem. The wrong options misdescribe who uses them, exaggerate what donations can do or reverse the advice services.
keyPoints: Food banks have changed from stopgaps into permanent fixtures.
More working families use them as living costs rise, and some offer advice.
Organisers say tins cannot solve poverty, so policy must change.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: When ferry workers went on strike, the island's shops ran short of fresh milk and bread within days. Some residents criticised the strikers, while others blamed the company for refusing to negotiate. Islanders soon set up a swap system, with families exchanging surplus vegetables for essentials. The dispute ended after ten days with a modest pay rise. Afterwards, many residents said the episode showed how dependent the island is on a single transport link.
options: The company agreed to the strikers' demands within the first day.
Residents blamed the strikers for the shortages of milk and bread.
The strike ended after residents refused to swap food with each other.
A ferry strike exposed the island's reliance on a single link.
quests.correctAnswer: A ferry strike exposed the island's reliance on a single link.
quests.hint: Identify the event and the lesson people drew from it.
quests.explanation: The strike caused shortages, people adapted through sharing, and the experience highlighted the island's vulnerability. The wrong options reverse residents' behaviour and opinions or the time and terms of the settlement.
keyPoints: A ferry strike caused shortages in the island's shops.
Residents blamed different sides and created a food-swap system.
The ten-day dispute highlighted the island's reliance on one link.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A company noticed that most of its cyber-security incidents began when staff clicked on convincing fake emails. Instead of sending another lecture, it began sending harmless practice phishing messages and gave immediate feedback to anyone who clicked. Click rates dropped from twenty percent to five within a year. Some employees resented being tested, so the company now reports only group figures. Security officers say a calm culture encourages people to report suspicious emails early.
options: The company stopped email training after the practice test succeeded so well.
Click rates rose after the company introduced harmless practice messages and lectures for staff.
Practice phishing tests reduced risky clicks, and a supportive approach encourages early reporting.
Employees who clicked were publicly named and blamed in front of their colleagues.
quests.correctAnswer: Practice phishing tests reduced risky clicks, and a supportive approach encourages early reporting.
quests.hint: Find the method, the result and the adjustment that followed employee reaction.
quests.explanation: Practice with feedback cut errors, and reporting only group figures responds to staff resentment. The wrong options reverse the click rate, the treatment of individuals and the training decision.
keyPoints: Most incidents started when staff clicked fake emails.
Harmless practice messages with instant feedback cut click rates to five percent.
The company now reports group figures to keep the culture calm.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: The library's makerspace lets members use 3D printers, sewing machines and soldering tools. Teenagers arrive after school to design phone cases and small robots. Retired engineers volunteer to mentor them, and the two groups often learn from each other. Librarians say the space has changed how the public sees the library, from a place for books to a place for making things. Funding is limited, however, and machines break more often than expected.
options: A library makerspace connects generations and broadens the library's role and upkeep is difficult.
The library has replaced its books with equipment for making things and mending.
Retired engineers use the space for their hobbies while teenagers act as their mentors.
The makerspace charges high fees for sessions on the 3D printers and machines.
quests.correctAnswer: A library makerspace connects generations and broadens the library's role and upkeep is difficult.
quests.hint: Keep the users, the benefit and the practical drawback in view.
quests.explanation: The space brings teenagers and retirees together and redefines the library, but it needs more support. The wrong options reverse the mentoring roles, add fees or claim books were removed.
keyPoints: The makerspace offers 3D printers, sewing machines and soldering tools.
Teenagers and retired engineers learn from each other.
It changes how people see the library, but funding and repairs are problems.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A rail company publishes punctuality figures for every route, and passengers use them to choose services. Some routes have improved because managers know they will be compared publicly. Others have found ways to appear punctual, for example by lengthening scheduled journey times. A regulator now requires companies to report against the original timetable as well. Passengers welcome the change, though some doubt that any single figure can capture the real experience of a journey.
options: Passengers believe that one figure captures the whole experience of a journey.
Published punctuality data spurs improvement and can be gamed so rules changed.
Punctuality figures were withdrawn by the regulator because passengers ignored them.
Companies shortened scheduled journey times so that trains would appear punctual.
quests.correctAnswer: Published punctuality data spurs improvement and can be gamed so rules changed.
quests.hint: Notice the benefit of the data and the way it can be manipulated.
quests.explanation: Public data spurs improvement, but lengthened timetables can hide problems, so regulators add a stricter measure. The wrong options reverse the data's use, the timetable trick and passengers' doubts.
keyPoints: Rail firms publish punctuality figures that passengers use.
Some improve, while others lengthen scheduled times to look punctual.
A regulator now requires reports against the original timetable.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: A dry coastal city has turned to desalination to secure drinking water. The plants remove salt from seawater using reverse osmosis, and they now supply nearly a third of the city's needs. The process is energy-intensive, and the leftover brine can harm marine life if released carelessly. Engineers are experimenting with solar power to cut energy costs and with diffusers that spread the brine more widely. Water managers say desalination is a useful safety net but not a substitute for saving water.
options: The plants supply the entire drinking water needs of the coastal city.
Desalination secures water for a dry city and demands careful management.
Water managers advise relying on desalination instead of saving water at home.
Desalination uses little energy and leaves harmless by-products in the sea.
quests.correctAnswer: Desalination secures water for a dry city and demands careful management.
quests.hint: Recognise that the writer treats the technology as useful but incomplete.
quests.explanation: The plants provide a substantial share of the city's water, while energy and brine issues need solutions and conservation remains necessary. The wrong options deny costs, exaggerate supply or contradict managers' advice.
keyPoints: A dry coastal city uses desalination for nearly a third of its water.
The process needs much energy and produces brine that can harm marine life.
Solar power and diffusers are being tested, and saving water is still needed.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: Cycling helmets are a subject of lasting disagreement. Studies show that helmets reduce the risk of serious head injury in a crash. Some campaigners argue that compulsory helmet laws discourage people from cycling, which reduces the health benefits of exercise. Others point out that helmets are an inexpensive precaution while roads remain dangerous. Cities that have built protected lanes report fewer injuries without compulsion, suggesting that infrastructure may matter more than the rules governing equipment.
options: Cities with protected lanes report more injuries than before they built them.
Studies show helmets increase the risk of serious head injury in most crashes.
Helmets protect riders and protected lanes may improve safety more than compulsory rules.
Campaigners argue that compulsory helmets encourage more people to take up cycling.
quests.correctAnswer: Helmets protect riders and protected lanes may improve safety more than compulsory rules.
quests.hint: See how the paragraph moves from individual protection to a broader conclusion.
quests.explanation: Helmets help in crashes, laws may reduce cycling, and protected lanes reduce injuries, so infrastructure looks important. The wrong options reverse the studies, the campaigners' claim and the evidence on lanes.
keyPoints: Helmets lower the risk of serious head injury in crashes.
Compulsion may discourage cycling, but helmets are cheap protection.
Protected lanes cut injuries without compulsion.

quests.instruction: Choose the best summary for the paragraph.
quests.passage: After the school closures, many children fell behind in reading and mathematics, and the gap between richer and poorer pupils grew. Governments funded small-group tutoring, which research shows to be more effective than large classes. Yet take-up has been uneven, since the schools with the most need often struggle to find tutors. Some have recruited university students, while others use online tutors. The concern now is that a temporary fund will not close a gap that took years to widen.
options: Tutoring helps pupils catch up and uneven access and short funding limit it.
Schools with the greatest need have found tutors most readily in the region.
Governments have committed lasting funding that will close the learning gap.
Small-group tutoring is less effective than teaching large classes, according to research.
quests.correctAnswer: Tutoring helps pupils catch up and uneven access and short funding limit it.
quests.hint: Give the remedy and the reasons it may fall short.
quests.explanation: Tutoring works, but shortages of tutors and temporary funding may prevent it from closing a long-standing gap. The wrong options reverse effectiveness, the difficulty in poorer schools and the funding commitment.
keyPoints: School closures widened the reading and maths gap between richer and poorer pupils.
Small-group tutoring works well but is unevenly available.
A temporary fund may not close a gap that took years to grow.
